en: The national flower sampaguita releases its strongest sweet fragrance at night to attract its primary pollinators, sphinx moths.
Indigenous Ifugao farmers maintain the Banaue Rice Terraces by channeling mountain rainwater through an ancient, gravity-fed stone irrigation system.
During the Lucban Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate house exteriors with kiping, which are vibrant, leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice.
National Scientist Angel Alcala helped restore Philippine coral reefs by establishing community-managed marine sanctuaries that visibly increased local fish populations.
The Philippine eagle, the national bird, features a distinctive crest of specialized brown feathers that it raises when alarmed.
The historic 1911 eruption of Taal Volcano created Volcano Island, a landmass visibly rising from the waters of Taal Lake.
Artisans in the Bicol region extract strong fibers from the native abaca plant to weave traditional sinamay fabric.
The carabao, the national animal, wallows in mud to cool down because it lacks sufficient functional sweat glands.
National Scientist Ramon Barba discovered that spraying mango trees with potassium nitrate causes them to bloom predictably out of season.
Dinagyang festival dancers in Iloilo wear vibrant costumes adorned with locally sourced natural materials like dyed feathers and seashells.
The government protects the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site where colorful coral atolls are visible above water.
Following typhoons, Filipinos practice bayanihan by collectively clearing fallen tree branches and debris from their local neighborhood streets.
